# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS)
Description: The Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS) is sponsored by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau. The MHS produces monthly regional estimates of the average sales price for new manufactured homes and more detailed annual estimates including selected characteristics of new manufactured homes. In addition, MHS produces monthly estimates of homes shipped by status. The statistics on shipments of new manufactured homes are produced by the Institute for Building Technology and Safety (IBTS). They are rounded in the month of release and unrounded in subsequent months. Both not seasonally adjusted and seasonally adjusted annual rates of shipment estimates of new manufactured homes are released monthly.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Manufactured Housing Survey comprehensively. Let me start with several searches.I have solid core information. Let me gather more details on IBTS's role, data access formats, and users.# Research Report: Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS)

## 1. Verification of Your Description

Your description is **accurate**, with a few refinements worth noting:

- ✅ Sponsored by HUD, conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau — correct.
- ✅ Monthly regional average sales prices for new manufactured homes; more detailed annual characteristics — correct.
- ✅ Shipment statistics produced by the **Institute for Building Technology and Safety (IBTS)**, rounded at first release and unrounded in later revisions — correct.
- ✅ Both not-seasonally-adjusted and seasonally adjusted annual rates (SAAR) of shipments released monthly — correct.
- ⚠️ Refinement: The monthly average sales price series in its *current form* begins with the August 2014 methodology redesign; earlier monthly price data exist in a discontinued "old series" (1980–2013) that Census explicitly warns is **not comparable** to the current series.
- ⚠️ Addition: An annual **Public Use File (PUF) microdata** product has been released since 2014 — a key fact for data librarians and data scientists that your description omits.

---

## 2. What the Dataset Is

The MHS is the federal government's primary statistical instrument on **new HUD-code manufactured homes** — factory-built housing constructed to the federal Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards (24 CFR Part 3280), in effect since June 15, 1976. Coverage includes *all* new manufactured homes that receive federal inspection at the factory (i.e., homes bearing the red HUD certification label).

**Core outputs:**

| Product | Geography | Frequency | History |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total shipments (IBTS counts, NSA + SAAR) | National, state | Monthly & annual | Back to 1959 |
| Shipments by status (sold/placed, intended for sale, nonresidential/other) | National | Monthly | January 2014–present |
| Average sales price (sold/placed or intended for sale) | Regional (monthly); national, region, division, state (annual) | Monthly & annual | Current series 2014–present; old series 1980–2013 (incomparable) |
| Selected characteristics (square footage, bedrooms, titling, foundation/footings/piers, placement location, leased status, etc.) | Regional | Annual | 1980–present |
| Public Use File microdata (one record per sampled home, with weights and imputation flags) | Regional | Annual | 2014–present |
| Cost & size comparison: manufactured vs. new single-family site-built homes | National | Annual | Recent years |

Notably, the MHS's manufactured home shipments series is a component of the Census Bureau's widely watched housing-starts ecosystem and feeds the manufactured-housing portion of new residential construction statistics.

---

## 3. Who Publishes It — The Three-Way Institutional Structure

1. **HUD (sponsor/funder).** The Office of Policy Development and Research (PD&R), through HUD USER, sponsors and funds the survey and uses its outputs. HUD also hosts the dataset on the **HUD USER web portal** (huduser.gov/portal/datasets/mhs), a mirror/distribution point separate from Census.
2. **U.S. Census Bureau (statistical collector).** Census selects the sample, mails questionnaires (Form C-MH-9A) to dealers, collects and imputes responses, produces estimates and the PUF, and publishes all tabulations at census.gov/programs-surveys/mhs.
3. **IBTS (Institute for Building Technology and Safety).** A nonprofit that has served as HUD's contract monitoring agent for the federal manufactured housing program for ~50 years (originally as the National Conference of States on Building Codes and Standards, NCSBCS). IBTS maintains the universe of HUD label/data-plate records from manufacturers' production reports (the sole source of this administrative data since 1976) and produces the monthly **shipment and production counts** that form both the published shipment statistics and the MHS sampling frame.

**Oversight:** The survey operates under **OMB Control Number 2528-0029** (Paperwork Reduction Act clearance), renewed periodically through Federal Register 60-day/30-day notices (e.g., March 11, 2022; March 6, 2025). These notices are valuable provenance documents: they describe respondent burden (~400 dealers contacted monthly), methods, and stated uses.

---

## 4. Legal Authority and Mandate

The survey's statutory footing rests on several pillars:

- **42 U.S.C. § 5424 note (Housing and Community Development Act of 1980)** — the core mandate. It directs the HUD Secretary to take actions necessary to ensure the public is aware of the distinctions among types of factory-built housing, and authorizes collecting and reporting manufactured home sales and price information for the nation, Census regions, states, and selected metropolitan areas, including monitoring whether new homes are placed on **owned versus rented lots** — a central affordable-housing policy question.
- **Title 13 U.S.C. § 8(b)** — authorizes the Census Bureau to conduct the survey on HUD's behalf (reimbursable/sponsored survey authority).
- **12 U.S.C. § 1701z-1** — HUD research authority.
- **Title 13 U.S.C. § 9** — guarantees **confidentiality**: responses may be used only for statistical purposes, which is why the survey is **voluntary** (not mandatory like some other Census programs).
- **Housing and Economic Recovery Act (HERA) of 2008, § 2145(b)** — a concrete downstream mandate: HUD must develop an indexing methodology to **annually adjust Title I manufactured home loan limits**, and that index is built on MHS price data. The resulting rule is "Indexing Methodology for Title I Manufactured Home Loan Limits" (implemented via Title I Letter TI-480 for loans from March 3, 2009).
- **Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. Ch. 35)** — governs OMB clearance.

---

## 5. History and Methodological Evolution

Understanding the series breaks is essential for any analyst:

- **1959–present:** Shipment counts (from IBTS's predecessor administrative systems) — the longest continuous series.
- **1974:** The monthly survey begins. **1974–1979 methodology:** a sample of dealers in 137 geographic areas (primary sampling units) contacted monthly about homes received, placed, and held in inventory.
- **1980–2013 (the "old series"):** a monthly sample of shipped units; dealers contacted **by telephone repeatedly each month until the unit was placed**. Annual characteristics tables begin in 1980. Census states plainly that these data **are not comparable** to the current series.
- **January 2010:** Sample redesign — from a 1-in-40 systematic sample to the current fixed-size design.
- **August 2014 (major redesign):** Dealers are now contacted **once, four months after shipment**, and asked the unit's status; they report actual sales price if sold/placed for residential use, or *intended* sales price if still intended for sale. This is why published "average sales price" blends actual and intended prices. The 4-month reference lag also explains why monthly data appear several months behind the shipment month.
- **January 2021:** Questionnaire revised to identify **leased units**, better distinguish placed vs. not-yet-placed units, and update characteristics questions (e.g., foundation question replaced by **footings** and **piers** items) to align with industry standards. Census says methodology was unchanged, but the PUF documentation warns that the SECURED variable differs from prior years.

**Current design in brief:** Each month IBTS supplies Census a frame listing all new HUD-inspected home sections shipped (Canadian-destined and FEMA-only units removed). A systematic sample of fixed size (~405 homes/month, drawn without replacement within each of the four Census regions) is selected; the sampling unit is the section, the tabulation unit is the home. Dealers are mailed Form C-MH-9A ~4 months post-shipment (mail, fax, or phone response; ~11 business days of collection). Missing items (status, destination, leased status, dimensions, bedrooms) are filled via **hot-deck imputation**; price is imputed via a **regression model on square footage and section type**. Weights are calibrated so estimated shipments equal IBTS published single- and multi-section control totals. Seasonally adjusted annual rates are revised each year with the April release (current year + five prior years). Total shipment counts are revised for the prior two months each release; price/status estimates are **not revised** in regular practice.

---

## 6. Who Uses It, and Why (Public Benefits)

Documented users and uses (from Census/HUD/OMB filings and federal rulemakings):

- **HUD:** monitors total new housing production and affordability; determines fair market values and rents; tracks owned-vs.-rented lot placements; and — statutorily required — **indexes Title I manufactured home loan limits annually** using MHS price data.
- **Bureau of Economic Analysis:** an input to **residential fixed investment** in U.S. GDP estimates.
- **Department of Energy:** cited in energy conservation standards rulemakings for manufactured housing (shipment data used in technical support documents).
- **FEMA:** the frame/status categories explicitly track FEMA units (relevant to disaster-housing logistics).
- **Trade associations** (e.g., Manufactured Housing Institute) and **manufacturers/suppliers:** market analysis, price and characteristics trend monitoring; **trade press** routinely cites the estimates.
- **Researchers and advocates:** Manufactured housing is the largest source of **unsubsidized affordable housing** in the U.S. (~94,500 new homes shipped in 2020, per the OMB filing). MHS is the authoritative source for work on affordable housing supply, chattel lending and titling reform, land-lease community issues, and zoning/siting policy — the data directly address the congressional concern about whether homes are placed on owned or rented land.
- **The general public:** the survey exists, per its authorizing statute, so the public understands the distinctions among factory-built housing types.

---

## 7. Access, Formats, and Preservation Notes

**Access points:**
- Census Bureau program page: census.gov/programs-surveys/mhs (latest monthly/annual tables, time-series data tools covering current series and old series 1980–2013, technical documentation, questionnaires C-MH-9A 2014–2020 and 2021–present).
- HUD USER dataset mirror: huduser.gov/portal/datasets/mhs.
- **Public Use Files (PUF), 2014–2025:** downloadable microdata, ~4,800–4,900 records/year (one per sampled home), with weights (WEIGHT, WGTADJ), disclosure-protected variables (PRICE and SQFT top/bottom-coded; bedrooms collapsed to ≤2 / ≥3; prices rounded on a sliding scale), and eleven "j" imputation-flag variables. Released annually (2025 PUF released June 2026 under approval ID CBDRB-FY26-0221).
- Formats are primarily Excel/PDF tables and flat microdata files; there is no dedicated MHS API endpoint — analysts typically download files or use Census's time-series tools.

**Limitations data scientists should flag:**
- Small monthly sample (~405 homes) → monthly regional price estimates carry substantial sampling error.
- Voluntary response with heavy imputation; status measured only at the 4-month mark.
- Price series mixes actual and intended sales prices.
- Pre-2014 data are structurally non-comparable; 2021 questionnaire changes affect some characteristics (esp. SECURED, foundation/footings/piers, leased).
- Monthly estimates are at regional level only; state-level prices are annual.

**Preservationist notes:**
- The dataset has already been archived independently — e.g., a copy exists on **DataLumos** (ICPSR's community archive for at-risk government data), indicating recognized preservation demand.
- Key preservation targets: annual PUFs + their PDF documentation, both questionnaire versions, the discontinued 1980–2013 old-series tables (available only on legacy "previous data" pages, the most fragile component), IBTS monthly shipment summaries, and the Federal Register ICR notices (60-day/30-day, OMB 2528-0029) which document purpose, burden, and authority across administrations.
- Because HUD sponsors and Census conducts, the dataset depends on interagency funding agreements — a structural vulnerability typical of sponsor-funded surveys and worth monitoring for continuity.

---

## 8. Summary Assessment

The MHS is a small-sample, high-policy-leverage dataset: the sole federal statistical series on the prices, characteristics, and placement patterns of new HUD-code manufactured homes, with shipment counts reaching back to 1959. Its authority traces to the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980 and HERA 2008; its integrity rests on the HUD–Census–IBTS triad; and its outputs flow into GDP accounts, federally mandated loan-limit indexing, DOE rulemakings, and affordable-housing policy debates. For preservation and reuse, the highest priorities are the annual PUF microdata, the incomparable pre-2014 series (which requires careful provenance labeling), and the survey's Federal Register documentation trail.

Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability

- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability

- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.

- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

I'll research the current risk context for the MHS, including Census Bureau and HUD staffing/funding, ICR status, publication continuity, and any recent policy actions.Now let me research HUD's budget and staffing situation, the MHS ICR renewal status, and shutdown impacts.The staffing tracker is archived and JavaScript-driven, so I'll rely on news and CRS sources. One more check on the enacted FY2026 funding level for HUD's Research & Technology account (which funds the MHS):I now have sufficient evidence for the assessment. Here is the complete risk report.

# Risk Assessment: Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS)

## Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for each level:**
- *Gone/High Risk:* No evidence. No historical files have been removed.
- *Moderate Risk:* No evidence of removed data elements. The old series (1980–2013) remains posted with clear non-comparability warnings — a documentation choice, not a removal.
- *No Known Issue:* As of late 2026, the full historical stack remains live on census.gov: monthly shipments 1959–2026, shipments-to-states 1994/2000–2026, the discontinued "old series" tables (1980–2013), annual characteristics 2014–2025 (released June 2026), and Public Use Files 2014–2025. An independent preservation copy exists on DataLumos (ICPSR). FRED/ALFRED also mirror the headline series.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** All prior-cycle data remain accessible and unaltered, with at least one independent archive copy.

## Future Data Availability

**Evidence for each level:**
- *Gone:* No — collection continues; the respondent portal shows an active due date (September 17, 2026).
- *High Risk:* Not met. The ICR (OMB 2528-0029) was renewed March 2025 as an "extension without change" and does not expire until **April 30, 2028**. No statutory deadline missed; no cycle skipped.
- *Moderate Risk:* Met. During the October–November 2025 lapse in appropriations, MHS releases were delayed and combined — Census's official release-date history flags the November 20 and December 9, 2025 releases with "*Due to lapse in appropriations release dates have been revised." This is a documented publication delay, and it demonstrates the survey's exposure to funding lapses (it is sponsor-funded via an annual HUD→Census interagency agreement, not a direct Census appropriation line).
- *No Known Issue:* Arguable — releases resumed, the schedule through April 2026+ is published, and 2026 releases have been on time (latest data current through mid-2026; annual release June 2026).

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The ICR is secure through 2028 and publication has fully resumed, but an actual multi-week publication delay occurred in late 2025, and the survey's dependence on annual sponsor funding plus appropriations continuity makes recurrence plausible.

## Data Quality

**Evidence for each level:**
- *Gone/High Risk:* No observed reductions. Monthly regional price/status estimates, state-level shipment tables, annual characteristics, and the 2025 PUF (4,859 records — full sample, with weights and imputation flags) were all released at normal granularity and frequency.
- *Moderate Risk:* Met. Emerging risks: (1) Census Bureau has lost ≥15% of staff and federal statistical agencies are "stretched thin" (ASA assessment, July 2026), degrading the institutional capacity behind imputation, seasonal adjustment, and disclosure review; (2) a June 2026 Trump administration order banning statistical "noise" at Census and BEA signals willingness to intervene in statistical methodology — the MHS PUF relies on top-coding/rounding rather than noise infusion, so direct impact is limited, but the precedent matters; (3) the proposed 32% cut to HUD's Research & Technology account would, if ever enacted, squeeze the surveys portfolio (AHS, SOC, SOMA, MHS, RHFS) competing for the same funds.
- *No Known Issue:* Defensible on observed output alone — nothing has been reduced yet.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Quality is currently intact, but staffing attrition and methodological-political interference constitute genuine emerging risk.

## Statutory Context

**Evidence for each level:**
- *High Risk:* Not met. Authorization is not vague, and there is no substitute collection — the MHS/IBTS pipeline is the *sole* federal source of new manufactured home shipment, price, and placement data.
- *Moderate Risk:* Not the best fit — the survey is arguably more than "not explicitly required."
- *No Known Issue:* Met. The collection is explicitly grounded in statute: 42 U.S.C. § 5424 note (Housing and Community Development Act of 1980) directs collection/reporting of manufactured home price and placement data including owned-vs.-rented lot status; HERA 2008 § 2145(b) **requires** HUD to index Title I manufactured home loan limits annually, a function Census's own Federal Register notices state is served by the MHS; the Federal Register ICR notices (2022, 2025) recite these authorities. The data feed a mandatory, ongoing federal program function with no alternative source.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** This is the dataset's strongest protective feature: explicit statutory mandates, a named programmatic use (Title I loan-limit indexing), and no substitute.

## Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for each level:**
- *Gone:* Not remotely met.
- *High Risk (≥40% staff lost / ≥1,000 lost / budget cut ≥20% / leadership removed):* Several criteria were *proposed or approached*: HUD announced plans to cut ~50% of staff, with PD&R (the MHS sponsor office) explicitly among offices to be "gutted" (NPR, Feb 2025; Senators' letter, Feb 20, 2025); one union leader cited ~75% targets for some offices. The President's FY2026 budget proposed cutting the R&T account that funds MHS by **32%** ($139M→$95M). Census Bureau Director Robert Santos resigned in February 2025 amid the administration transition (arguably "leadership removed"). HUD's FY2026 plan shows FTEs falling 8,597→6,340 (-26%) — below the 40% threshold.
- *Moderate Risk (10–39% staff lost / 500–999 lost / budget cut 10–19% / threatened leadership change):* Squarely met on confirmed outcomes: Census Bureau lost **at least 15%** of staff (AP/ASA report, 2026); ~100 Census employees received shutdown RIF notices (Oct 2025, Tucson); HUD had removed ~15% of staff by mid-March 2025 with RIFs totaling roughly 26% implemented/funded (Terner Center; NLIHC analysis of the House FY2026 bill). Six of 13 statistical agencies lost ≥1/3 of staff — system-wide degradation of the environment MHS depends on.
- *No Known Issue:* Not met, though note enacted budgets were relatively protective: FY2026 Census enacted at $1.490B (+$108M vs FY2025), and the final FY2026 THUD Act (P.L. 119-75, Feb 2026) increased HUD funding overall +12.6%, rejecting the deepest proposed cuts.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** Confirmed losses land in the 10–39% band for both responsible agencies, and enacted budgets were not cut. However, this rating sits close to High: the sponsoring office (PD&R) was specifically targeted for elimination-level cuts, the account funding MHS was proposed for a >20% cut, and agency leadership turnover has occurred. Continued monitoring is warranted.

## Policy

**Evidence for each level:**
- *Gone/High Risk:* Not met. The March 2025 ICR was a routine "extension without change," not a Presidential-Action-driven collection. No negative policy notes on the MHS pages; no content changes aligned with administration priorities (unlike e.g. cancelled surveys such as the 2026 Census of Governments classification survey).
- *Moderate Risk:* Only ambient risk — the administration has cancelled or altered other Census products without explanation (NPR, Apr 2025) and intervened in methodology via the June 2026 noise order.
- *No Known Issue:* Met. No changes since January 2025 to what MHS collects or publishes. Moreover, the administration's housing policy *favors* manufactured housing — Secretary Turner has championed manufactured housing deregulation as an affordability strategy, and the MHS's statutory loan-limit indexing function remains in active use — creating policy alignment that protects rather than threatens the survey.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** The MHS is arguably *benefiting* from current administration housing policy, though the broader pattern of abrupt changes at Census justifies watchfulness.

## Summary

| Category | Risk Level |
|---|---|
| Historical Data Availability | **No Known Issue** |
| Future Data Availability | **Moderate Risk** (shutdown-driven delays occurred; ICR active through April 2028) |
| Data Quality | **Moderate Risk** (no reductions yet; staffing attrition and methodological interference are emerging risks) |
| Statutory Context | **No Known Issue** (explicit statutory mandate; required for Title I loan-limit indexing; no substitutes) |
| Staffing and Funding | **Moderate Risk** (15%+ losses at Census, ~26% at HUD; PD&R and its funding account specifically targeted, though worst-case cuts not enacted) |
| Policy | **No Known Issue** (no post-January 2025 changes; administration supportive of manufactured housing) |

**Overall judgment:** The MHS is a *low-to-moderate risk* dataset. Its statutory anchoring, active ICR through 2028, continued on-schedule publication, independent archival copies, and alignment with current housing policy are strong protective factors. Its principal vulnerabilities are structural rather than political: sponsor-funded status exposing it to appropriations lapses (demonstrated in late 2025), and its dependence on two agencies — HUD PD&R and the Census Bureau — that have both sustained double-digit staffing losses, with the sponsoring office having been an explicit target of the deepest proposed cuts. Preservationists should prioritize mirroring the annual PUFs, the 1980–2013 old-series tables, and the Federal Register ICR documentation trail while these remain freely available.
